title: Prepare new hires for nesting without removing their support
summary: Prepare new hires for supported live work with combined-task practice, a useful coach handoff and clear boundaries for independent decisions.
body_markdown:
Nesting gives new hires supervised experience with real customers. Practice beforehand should help them enter that stage prepared, while giving coaches a clearer view of where support is still needed. It should not become a reason to withdraw help before someone is ready.


## Find the moments that require coach intervention


Ask coaches which tasks repeatedly interrupt early live work. Separate questions about policy from trouble finding information, choosing a system action or managing the conversation while completing the task. A knowledge test can show that someone remembers a rule without showing that they can use it with a customer waiting.


Choose a small set of common or consequential situations for preparation. Keep unusual exceptions on the escalation path if they cannot be practiced credibly. The objective is to make expected work familiar and make the limits of independence explicit.


## Rehearse the combined task


Let learners practice listening, navigating the relevant workflow, making a decision and explaining it together. Include finding approved guidance and asking for help at the right point. Treat appropriate escalation as a skill rather than a failure. A representative who recognizes an authorization limit may be better prepared than someone who completes the interaction confidently but takes an action they were not permitted to take.


## Create a handoff that a coach can use


Send a brief readiness record with each learner instead of relying on a completion flag. Agree the record with the receiving operations team before the cohort reaches nesting.


Handoff item What the coach needs


Practiced work Tasks attempted and the conditions included


Observed performance What the learner could do, with relevant evidence


Remaining support Decisions or steps that still required prompts


Escalation boundaries Situations requiring approval or immediate help


Next checkpoint Named reviewer and when live-work readiness will be reconsidered


## A fictional example: moving onto a billing queue


A new representative can explain invoices but needs help when a customer disputes a charge during a call. Before nesting, the trainer assigns practice that combines finding the invoice, checking the adjustment policy and explaining the decision. The learner handles a routine correction but still needs a prompt when the requested amount exceeds their authority. The handoff records that distinction. During nesting, the coach stays available for approvals and checks the learner's early interactions; the simulation result does not authorize independent adjustments outside the role's limits.


## Review support needs before changing the program


Record the kind of help coaches provide, not just the total time they spend. Useful categories include policy clarification, navigation, reassurance and escalation decisions. Look for repeated issues that could be addressed before the next cohort enters live work, and keep time for coaching on situations that require judgment.


If you test a revised preparation program, compare cohorts carefully. Differences in prior experience, queue difficulty or coach availability can affect the result. Review service outcomes and learner experience alongside coaching effort before shortening nesting or changing staffing. Simulation evidence can inform that decision, but it cannot establish on its own that someone will perform consistently with real customers.
